claim: Cytokinesis is powered by constriction of an actomyosin contractile ring.
source: Cytokinesis, the physical division of one cell into two, is powered by constriction of an actomyosin contractile ring.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the mechanism of cytokinesis.

claim: It has long been assumed that all animal cells divide by a similar molecular mechanism.
source: It has long been assumed that all animal cells divide by a similar molecular mechanism, but growing evidence suggests that cytokinetic regulation in individual cell types has more variation than previously realized.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical scientific consensus.

claim: Growing evidence suggests that cytokinetic regulation in individual cell types has more variation than previously realized.
source: It has long been assumed that all animal cells divide by a similar molecular mechanism, but growing evidence suggests that cytokinetic regulation in individual cell types has more variation than previously realized.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing cytokinetic diversity.

claim: In the four-cell Caenorhabditis elegans embryo, each blastomere has a distinct cell fate specified by conserved pathways.
source: In the four-cell Caenorhabditis elegans embryo, each blastomere has a distinct cell fate, specified by conserved pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: Cell-type-specific variation in the cytokinetic requirement for forminCYK-1-dependent F-actin cytoskeleton was identified in the four-cell C. elegans embryo.
source: Using fast-acting temperature-sensitive mutants and acute drug treatment, we identified cell-type-specific variation in the cytokinetic requirement for a robust forminCYK-1-dependent filamentous-actin (F-actin) cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using temperature-sensitive mutants and drug treatments.

claim: In P2 cells, cytokinetic variation is cell-intrinsically regulated.
source: In one cell (P2), this cytokinetic variation is cell-intrinsically regulated, whereas in another cell (EMS) this variation is cell-extrinsically regulated, dependent on both SrcSRC-1 signaling and direct contact with its neighbor cell, P2.
evidence: This is supported by blastomere isolation experiments showing P2 cells maintain cytokinetic protection when isolated.

claim: In EMS cells, cytokinetic variation is cell-extrinsically regulated, dependent on both SrcSRC-1 signaling and direct contact with P2.
source: In one cell (P2), this cytokinetic variation is cell-intrinsically regulated, whereas in another cell (EMS) this variation is cell-extrinsically regulated, dependent on both SrcSRC-1 signaling and direct contact with its neighbor cell, P2.
evidence: This is supported by blastomere pairing experiments and RNAi depletion of SrcSRC-1.

claim: Both cell-intrinsic and -extrinsic mechanisms control cytokinetic variation in individual cell types.
source: Thus, both cell-intrinsic and -extrinsic mechanisms control cytokinetic variation in individual cell types and can protect against division failure when the contractile ring is weakened.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on P2 and EMS cells.

claim: Cell-intrinsic and -extrinsic mechanisms can protect against division failure when the contractile ring is weakened.
source: Thus, both cell-intrinsic and -extrinsic mechanisms control cytokinetic variation in individual cell types and can protect against division failure when the contractile ring is weakened.
evidence: This is supported by data showing EMS and P2 cells successfully divide when forminCYK-1 is inhibited.

claim: In animal cells, cytokinesis is driven by the equatorial constriction of an actomyosin contractile ring composed of diaphanous family formin-nucleated F-actin and the motor myosin-II.
source: In animal cells, cytokinesis is driven by the equatorial constriction of an actomyosin contractile ring, composed of diaphanous family formin-nucleated F-actin and the motor myosin-II (for review see [Cheffings et al., 2016; D'Avino et al., 2015; Green et al., 2012; Mandato et al., 2000; Mishima, 2016; Pollard, 2010]).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple review citations.

claim: Cytokinesis failure results in a binucleate tetraploid (polyploid) cell.
source: Cytokinesis failure, which results in a binucleate tetraploid (polyploid) cell, can lead to human diseases including blood syndromes, neurological disorders, and cancer (Bione et al., 1998; Moulding et al., 2007; Dieterich et al., 2009; Vinciguerra et al., 2010; Lacroix and Maddox, 2012; Iolascon et al., 2013; Liljeholm et al., 2013; Ferrer et al., 2014; Ganem et al., 2014, 2007; Tormos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cellular consequence of cytokinesis failure.

claim: Cytokinesis failure can lead to human diseases including blood syndromes, neurological disorders, and cancer.
source: Cytokinesis failure, which results in a binucleate tetraploid (polyploid) cell, can lead to human diseases including blood syndromes, neurological disorders, and cancer (Bione et al., 1998; Moulding et al., 2007; Dieterich et al., 2009; Vinciguerra et al., 2010; Lacroix and Maddox, 2012; Iolascon et al., 2013; Liljeholm et al., 2013; Ferrer et al., 2014; Ganem et al., 2014, 2007; Tormos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies linking cytokinesis failure to disease.

claim: The functional regulation of cytokinesis has more diversity than previously appreciated.
source: While it has long been assumed that all animal cells divide by a similar molecular mechanism, it is becoming increasingly clear that the functional regulation of cytokinesis has more diversity, or variation in mechanistic and regulatory pathways, than previously appreciated (Herszterg et al., 2014; Guillot and Lecuit, 2013; Founounou et al., 2013; Herszterg et al., 2013; De Santis Puzzonia et al., 2016; Choudhary et al., 2013; Wheatley et al., 1997; Stopp et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating cytokinetic diversity.

claim: In many animals, specific cell types or cell lineages are programmed to fail in cytokinesis and become bi- or multi-nucleate.
source: In many animals (including humans), specific cell types or cell lineages within the organism are programmed to fail in cytokinesis and become bi- or multi-nucleate (e.g. osteoclasts in bone, megakaryocytes in blood, cardiomyocytes in the heart, hepatocytes in the liver) (Lacroix and Maddox, 2012; Tormos et al., 2015; Zimmet and Ravid, 2000; Duncan, 2013; Takegahara et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on specific cell types that normally undergo cytokinesis failure.

claim: In some cell types, cytokinesis failure occurs normally during development and/or homeostasis.
source: Thus, in some cell types, cytokinesis failure occurs normally during development and/or homeostasis and, in other cell types, cytokinesis failure can be pathogenic (Lacroix and Maddox, 2012; Tormos et al., 2015; Zimmet and Ravid, 2000; Duncan, 2013; Takegahara et al., 2016), indicating a high degree of cellular variation in both the regulation of cytokinesis and the consequences of cytokinesis failure.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on normal and pathogenic cytokinesis failure.

claim: In other cell types, cytokinesis failure can be pathogenic.
source: Thus, in some cell types, cytokinesis failure occurs normally during development and/or homeostasis and, in other cell types, cytokinesis failure can be pathogenic (Lacroix and Maddox, 2012; Tormos et al., 2015; Zimmet and Ravid, 2000; Duncan, 2013; Takegahara et al., 2016), indicating a high degree of cellular variation in both the regulation of cytokinesis and the consequences of cytokinesis failure.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on pathogenic cytokinesis failure.

claim: There is a high degree of cellular variation in both the regulation of cytokinesis and the consequences of cytokinesis failure.
source: Thus, in some cell types, cytokinesis failure occurs normally during development and/or homeostasis and, in other cell types, cytokinesis failure can be pathogenic (Lacroix and Maddox, 2012; Tormos et al., 2015; Zimmet and Ravid, 2000; Duncan, 2013; Takegahara et al., 2016), indicating a high degree of cellular variation in both the regulation of cytokinesis and the consequences of cytokinesis failure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on normal and pathogenic cytokinesis failure.

claim: Organism-wide mutations in cytokinesis genes are associated with cell-type-specific disruption of cell division in flies, fish, worms, rodents, and humans.
source: As further support for cell-type-specific cytokinetic variation, genomic analysis has revealed that organism-wide mutations in cytokinesis genes are associated with cell-type-specific disruption of cell division in flies, fish, worms, rodents, and even humans (Bione et al., 1998; Moulding et al., 2007; Vinciguerra et al., 2010; Liljeholm et al., 2013; Sgrò et al., 2016; Taniguchi et al., 2014; Muzzi et al., 2009; Giansanti et al., 2004; Paw et al., 2003; Menon et al., 2014; Morita et al., 2005; Jackson et al., 2011; Di Cunto et al., 2000; LoTurco et al., 2003; Ackman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genomic studies across different organisms.

claim: An autosomal dominant mutation in the human kinesin-6 MKLP1 leads to congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type III.
source: For example, an autosomal dominant mutation in the human kinesin-6 MKLP1, a protein thought to be essential for cytokinesis in all animal cells (Glotzer, 2009), leads to congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type III (Liljeholm et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on MKLP1 mutations.

claim: MKLP1 is a protein thought to be essential for cytokinesis in all animal cells.
source: For example, an autosomal dominant mutation in the human kinesin-6 MKLP1, a protein thought to be essential for cytokinesis in all animal cells (Glotzer, 2009), leads to congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type III (Liljeholm et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Glotzer 2009.

claim: Patients with MKLP1 mutations have multinucleated erythroblasts due to cytokinesis failure but are otherwise asymptomatic.
source: These patients have multinucleated erythroblasts due to a failure in cytokinesis but are otherwise asymptomatic, indicating that cells in other tissues and organs divide successfully (Liljeholm et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liljeholm et al., 2013.

claim: Cells in other tissues and organs divide successfully in patients with MKLP1 mutations.
source: These patients have multinucleated erythroblasts due to a failure in cytokinesis but are otherwise asymptomatic, indicating that cells in other tissues and organs divide successfully (Liljeholm et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that patients are otherwise asymptomatic.

claim: Mutations in Citron Kinase are associated with cytokinesis failure specifically in neuronal precursor cells, leading to multinucleated neurons and microcephaly in mice, rats, and human patients.
source: Mutations in Citron Kinase are associated with cytokinesis failure specifically in neuronal precursor cells, leading to multinucleated neurons and microcephaly in mice, rats, and human patients, but the development of other tissues and organs is not grossly disrupted (Sgrò et al., 2016; Di Cunto et al., 2000; Ackman et al., 2007; Harding et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016; Basit et al., 2016; Shaheen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on Citron Kinase mutations.

claim: The development of other tissues and organs is not grossly disrupted in Citron Kinase mutants.
source: Mutations in Citron Kinase are associated with cytokinesis failure specifically in neuronal precursor cells, leading to multinucleated neurons and microcephaly in mice, rats, and human patients, but the development of other tissues and organs is not grossly disrupted (Sgrò et al., 2016; Di Cunto et al., 2000; Ackman et al., 2007; Harding et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016; Basit et al., 2016; Shaheen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Citron Kinase mutations.

claim: A mouse knockout of GAS2L3 dies shortly after birth due to specific defects in cardiomyocyte cytokinesis during heart development.
source: Moreover, a mouse knockout of the microtubule and actin-binding protein GAS2L3 dies shortly after birth due to specific defects in cardiomyocyte cytokinesis during heart development, but the overall development of other tissues is not affected (Stopp et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stopp et al., 2017.

claim: The overall development of other tissues is not affected in GAS2L3 knockout mice.
source: Moreover, a mouse knockout of the microtubule and actin-binding protein GAS2L3 dies shortly after birth due to specific defects in cardiomyocyte cytokinesis during heart development, but the overall development of other tissues is not affected (Stopp et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stopp et al., 2017.

claim: Cell-type-specific mechanisms modulate the diversity of cytokinesis in animal cells.
source: These findings suggest that cell-type-specific mechanisms modulate the diversity of cytokinesis in animal cells, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms that underlie this diversity are poorly understood, even at a basic level.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited examples of cell-type-specific cytokinesis defects.

claim: The cellular and molecular mechanisms that underlie cytokinetic diversity are poorly understood.
source: These findings suggest that cell-type-specific mechanisms modulate the diversity of cytokinesis in animal cells, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms that underlie this diversity are poorly understood, even at a basic level.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Cell polarity proteins can promote robust cytokinesis during asymmetric cell division.
source: In support of cell-intrinsic regulation, we and others found that cell polarity proteins can promote robust cytokinesis during asymmetric cell division (Jordan et al., 2016; Cabernard et al., 2010; Roth et al., 2015), and asymmetrically inherited RNA granules in germ lineage cells contain a key splicing regulator involved in cytokinesis (Audhya et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on cell polarity and cytokinesis.

claim: Asymmetrically inherited RNA granules in germ lineage cells contain a key splicing regulator involved in cytokinesis.
source: In support of cell-intrinsic regulation, we and others found that cell polarity proteins can promote robust cytokinesis during asymmetric cell division (Jordan et al., 2016; Cabernard et al., 2010; Roth et al., 2015), and asymmetrically inherited RNA granules in germ lineage cells contain a key splicing regulator involved in cytokinesis (Audhya et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Audhya et al., 2005.

claim: Cell-cell adhesion junctions have been implicated in regulating contractile ring constriction in epithelial cells.
source: In support of extrinsic regulation, cell-cell adhesion junctions have been implicated in regulating contractile ring constriction in epithelial cells (Guillot and Lecuit, 2013; Founounou et al., 2013; Herszterg et al., 2013; Bourdages and Maddox, 2013; Pinheiro et al., 2017; Lázaro-Diéguez and Müsch, 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Daniel et al., 2018), and cell-fate signaling molecules, such as Wnt and Src, have been linked to cytokinesis in some contexts (Fumoto et al., 2012; Kasahara et al., 2007; Soeda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on cell-cell adhesion and cytokinesis.

claim: Cell-fate signaling molecules, such as Wnt and Src, have been linked to cytokinesis in some contexts.
source: In support of extrinsic regulation, cell-cell adhesion junctions have been implicated in regulating contractile ring constriction in epithelial cells (Guillot and Lecuit, 2013; Founounou et al., 2013; Herszterg et al., 2013; Bourdages and Maddox, 2013; Pinheiro et al., 2017; Lázaro-Diéguez and Müsch, 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Daniel et al., 2018), and cell-fate signaling molecules, such as Wnt and Src, have been linked to cytokinesis in some contexts (Fumoto et al., 2012; Kasahara et al., 2007; Soeda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Wnt and Src signaling in cytokinesis.

claim: The C. elegans four-cell embryo is a powerful, optically clear system to probe the mechanisms of cell-type-specific variation in cytokinesis.
source: The C. elegans four-cell embryo is a powerful, optically clear system to probe the mechanisms of cell-type-specific variation in cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental system used in the study.

claim: All four-cell divisions in C. elegans occur within a ~20 min time frame.
source: All four-cell divisions occur within a ~20 min time frame, and cytokinesis can easily be monitored in each individual blastomere, or cell within the embryo, by light microscopy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: Cytokinesis can easily be monitored in each individual blastomere in the C. elegans four-cell embryo by light microscopy.
source: All four-cell divisions occur within a ~20 min time frame, and cytokinesis can easily be monitored in each individual blastomere, or cell within the embryo, by light microscopy.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical feasibility of the experimental approach.

claim: Worm development follows a defined cell lineage pattern.
source: Worm development follows a defined cell lineage pattern (Sulston and Horvitz, 1977; Sulston et al., 1983), and the cell-fate patterning of each blastomere in the four-cell embryo is known (Rose and Gönczy, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to classic lineage studies.

claim: The cell-fate patterning of each blastomere in the four-cell C. elegans embryo is known.
source: Worm development follows a defined cell lineage pattern (Sulston and Horvitz, 1977; Sulston et al., 1983), and the cell-fate patterning of each blastomere in the four-cell embryo is known (Rose and Gönczy, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to a review.

claim: At the four-to-eight-cell division, each of the four cells are already specified to form distinct cell lineages by conserved, well-characterized cell-fate signaling pathways.
source: At the four-to-eight-cell division, each of the four cells are already specified to form distinct cell linages by conserved, well-characterized cell-fate signaling pathways (e.g. Notch/Delta, Wnt, Src; for review see [Rose and Gönczy, 2014; Priess, 2005; Bowerman, 1995]).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to reviews.

claim: The two-cell C. elegans embryo divides to form two anterior blastomeres, ABa and ABp, and two posterior blastomeres, EMS and P2.
source: The two-cell embryo divides to form two anterior blastomeres, ABa and ABp, and two posterior blastomeres, EMS and P2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: The anterior blastomeres ABa and ABp are born as identical sisters.
source: While the anterior blastomeres are born as identical sisters, activation of Notch family receptors in ABp by a Delta-like ligand on the surface of P2 induces ABp to adopt a different cell fate than ABa (Mickey et al., 1996; Bowerman et al., 1992; Mango et al., 1994; Moskowitz et al., 1994; Shelton and Bowerman, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: Activation of Notch family receptors in ABp by a Delta-like ligand on the surface of P2 induces ABp to adopt a different cell fate than ABa.
source: While the anterior blastomeres are born as identical sisters, activation of Notch family receptors in ABp by a Delta-like ligand on the surface of P2 induces ABp to adopt a different cell fate than ABa (Mickey et al., 1996; Bowerman et al., 1992; Mango et al., 1994; Moskowitz et al., 1994; Shelton and Bowerman, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on Notch signaling in C. elegans.

claim: The two posterior blastomeres, EMS and P2, are born from an asymmetric cell division.
source: The two posterior blastomeres, EMS and P2, are born from an asymmetric cell division and cell-cell contact-mediated Wnt and Src signaling between P2 and EMS promote asymmetric cell division and cell fate specification in both cells (Goldstein, 1992, 1993, 1995a, 1995b; Rocheleau et al., 1997; Thorpe et al., 1997; Bei et al., 2002; Arata et al., 2010; Schierenberg, 1987).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: Cell-cell contact-mediated Wnt and Src signaling between P2 and EMS promote asymmetric cell division and cell fate specification in both cells.
source: The two posterior blastomeres, EMS and P2, are born from an asymmetric cell division and cell-cell contact-mediated Wnt and Src signaling between P2 and EMS promote asymmetric cell division and cell fate specification in both cells (Goldstein, 1992, 1993, 1995a, 1995b; Rocheleau et al., 1997; Thorpe et al., 1997; Bei et al., 2002; Arata et al., 2010; Schierenberg, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on Wnt and Src signaling in C. elegans.

claim: In the four-cell C. elegans embryo, each cell has a unique cell identity and can be individually scored for contractile ring constriction during cytokinesis.
source: Therefore, in the four-cell C. elegans embryo, each cell has a unique cell identity and can be individually scored for contractile ring constriction during cytokinesis.
evidence: This is an inference from the established knowledge about C. elegans development and the technical feasibility of imaging.

claim: Fast-acting temperature-sensitive alleles were used to inactivate myosin-IINMY-2 and forminCYK-1 in the four-cell C. elegans embryo.
source: We used fast-acting temperature-sensitive (ts) alleles to inactivate two cytokinesis proteins essential for contractile ring constriction in the one-cell embryo (Davies et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2010): the motor myosin-II (NMY-2 in C. elegans, hereafter myosin-IINMY-2) and the diaphanous formin CYK-1 (hereafter forminCYK-1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Myosin-IINMY-2 and forminCYK-1 are essential for contractile ring constriction in the one-cell C. elegans embryo.
source: We used fast-acting temperature-sensitive (ts) alleles to inactivate two cytokinesis proteins essential for contractile ring constriction in the one-cell embryo (Davies et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2010): the motor myosin-II (NMY-2 in C. elegans, hereafter myosin-IINMY-2) and the diaphanous formin CYK-1 (hereafter forminCYK-1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cell-type-specific variation in four-cell embryos was identified in the molecular requirement for forminCYK-1, but not myosin-IINMY-2.
source: We identified cell-type-specific variation in four-cell embryos in the molecular requirement for forminCYK-1, but not myosin-IINMY-2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from temperature-sensitive mutant analysis.

claim: Cytokinesis in ABa and ABp blastomeres is sensitive to reduced forminCYK-1 activity.
source: Specifically, we found that while cytokinesis in two blastomeres, ABa and ABp, is sensitive to reduced forminCYK-1 activity, cytokinesis in the other two blastomeres, EMS and P2, is resistant to defects in forminCYK-1-mediated F-actin assembly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from temperature-sensitive mutant analysis.

claim: Cytokinesis in EMS and P2 blastomeres is resistant to defects in forminCYK-1-mediated F-actin assembly.
source: Specifically, we found that while cytokinesis in two blastomeres, ABa and ABp, is sensitive to reduced forminCYK-1 activity, cytokinesis in the other two blastomeres, EMS and P2, is resistant to defects in forminCYK-1-mediated F-actin assembly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from temperature-sensitive mutant analysis.

claim: Cytokinesis in ABa and ABp cells is sensitive to treatment with low doses of LatrunculinA.
source: Likewise, cytokinesis in ABa and ABp cells is sensitive to treatment with low doses of LatrunculinA (LatA), a drug that block F-actin polymerization, whereas cytokinesis in EMS and P2 cells is resistant to LatA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from LatA treatment experiments.

claim: Cytokinesis in EMS and P2 cells is resistant to LatrunculinA.
source: Likewise, cytokinesis in ABa and ABp cells is sensitive to treatment with low doses of LatrunculinA (LatA), a drug that block F-actin polymerization, whereas cytokinesis in EMS and P2 cells is resistant to LatA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from LatA treatment experiments.

source: Likewise, cytokinesis in ABa and ABp cells is sensitive to treatment with low doses of LatrunculinA (LatA), a drug that block F-actin polymerization, whereas cytokinesis in EMS and P2 cells is resistant to LatA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of action of LatrunculinA.

claim: EMS and P2 cells have greatly reduced F-actin levels at the division plane upon forminCYK-1 disruption.
source: We further found that EMS and P2 cells have greatly reduced F-actin levels at the division plane upon forminCYK-1 disruption, despite considerable and often successful equatorial constriction during cytokinesis, suggesting that cytokinesis in these cells is less dependent on F-actin in the contractile ring.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from F-actin imaging in formincyk-1(ts) mutants.

claim: EMS and P2 cells show considerable and often successful equatorial constriction during cytokinesis despite reduced F-actin levels upon forminCYK-1 disruption.
source: We further found that EMS and P2 cells have greatly reduced F-actin levels at the division plane upon forminCYK-1 disruption, despite considerable and often successful equatorial constriction during cytokinesis, suggesting that cytokinesis in these cells is less dependent on F-actin in the contractile ring.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from imaging cytokinesis in formincyk-1(ts) mutants.

claim: Cytokinesis in EMS and P2 cells is less dependent on F-actin in the contractile ring.
source: We further found that EMS and P2 cells have greatly reduced F-actin levels at the division plane upon forminCYK-1 disruption, despite considerable and often successful equatorial constriction during cytokinesis, suggesting that cytokinesis in these cells is less dependent on F-actin in the contractile ring.

source: We found that P2 cells are protected against cytokinesis failure after forminCYK-1 disruption even when isolated from the embryo, indicating cell-intrinsic regulation of cytokinesis, whereas EMS cells are not protected against cytokinesis failure upon isolation.

claim: P2 cytokinesis is subject to cell-intrinsic regulation.
source: We found that P2 cells are protected against cytokinesis failure after forminCYK-1 disruption even when isolated from the embryo, indicating cell-intrinsic regulation of cytokinesis, whereas EMS cells are not protected against cytokinesis failure upon isolation.

evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Cell isolation and blastomere pairing experiments revealed that P2 is protected against cytokinesis failure due to cell-intrinsic regulation and independent of contact with other blastomeres.
source: Cell isolation and blastomere pairing experiments revealed that P2 is protected against cytokinesis failure due to cell-intrinsic regulation and independent of contact with other blastomeres.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The early C. elegans four-cell embryo is established as a system to study cytokinetic diversity.

claim: At least in the early C. elegans embryo, both cell-intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms contribute to cell-type-specific cytokinetic diversity.

evidence: This is an inference from the observation that cells divide successfully despite undetectable F-actin enrichment.

claim: In EMS and P2 cells that divide successfully upon forminCYK-1 inactivation, contractile ring constriction progresses more slowly.

claim: EMS and P2 cells are utilizing a sub-optimal contractile ring when forminCYK-1 is inactivated.
source: In EMS and P2 cells that divide successfully upon forminCYK-1 inactivation, contractile ring constriction progresses more slowly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that these cells are utilizing a sub-optimal contractile ring.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that contractile ring constriction is slower.

claim: MyosinNMY-2 is still essential for cytokinesis in EMS and P2.
source: Indeed, myosinNMY-2 is still essential for cytokinesis in EMS and P2, indicating a 'normal' constricting actomyosin contractile ring is likely driving division in these blastomeres.
evidence: This is supported by the myosin-IInmy-2(ts) data showing all cells fail in cytokinesis.

claim: A 'normal' constricting actomyosin contractile ring is likely driving division in EMS and P2 blastomeres.
source: Indeed, myosinNMY-2 is still essential for cytokinesis in EMS and P2, indicating a 'normal' constricting actomyosin contractile ring is likely driving division in these blastomeres.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that myosinNMY-2 is essential.

claim: EMS and P2 blastomeres are able to divide successfully with a substantially weakened F-actin contractile ring.
source: Nonetheless, it is clear that, unlike one-cell embryos and ABa/ABp cells, EMS and P2 blastomeres are still somehow able to divide successfully with a substantially weakened F-actin contractile ring, whether weakened by inhibition of forminCYK-1 or application of low doses of Latrunculin A.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: EMS and P2 divide asymmetrically, whereas ABa and ABp divide symmetrically.
source: An obvious distinction of these more robustly dividing cells is that EMS and P2 divide asymmetrically, whereas ABa and ABp divide symmetrically (Rose and Gönczy, 2014; Arata et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Anterior-posterior cell polarity and the PAR proteins are essential for robust cytokinesis in the one-cell C. elegans embryo.
source: In the one-cell C. elegans embryo, we previously found that anterior-posterior cell polarity and the PAR proteins are essential for robust cytokinesis (Jordan et al., 2016).

source: The PAR proteins localize to opposing cortical domains in P2 but are not obviously asymmetrically distributed in EMS (Arata et al., 2010).

source: Little is known about cell polarity establishment and/or maintenance in EMS, but in P2, cell polarity is cell-intrinsically established, though proper orientation of polarity relative to the spindle is dependent on cell-extrinsic signaling from EMS (Arata et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arata et al., 2010.

claim: Whole embryo PAR protein disruption (by par-6(RNAi)) eliminates protection of cytokinesis in EMS and P2.

claim: In mammalian cultured cells, traction-mediated cytofission, driven by daughter cell elongation, crawling, and cell-substrate adhesion, can promote cell division in the absence of an actomyosin contractile ring.

evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on cytofission.

claim: Cytofission is not likely to be the main driver of cytokinesis in EMS and P2 cells.
source: Cytofission is not likely to be the main driver of cytokinesis in these cells since, even upon blastomere isolation, we do not observe cell crawling behavior or increased daughter cell elongation in EMS or P2.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that cell crawling and elongation are not observed.

claim: Polar cortical relaxation is proposed to facilitate actomyosin contractile ring constriction at the cell equator by reducing cortical contractility outside of the division plane in the polar regions of the cell.
source: Another possible driver of cytokinesis outside of the contractile ring is polar cortical relaxation, in which reduced cortical contractility outside of the division plane in the polar regions of the cell is proposed to facilitate actomyosin contractile ring constriction at the cell equator (Wolpert, 2014, 1960; Kunda et al., 2012; Rodrigues et al., 2015; Mangal et al., 2018; Lewellyn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on polar cortical relaxation.

claim: Polar cortical relaxation has been proposed to be regulated by Aurora A kinase activity, astral microtubules, and PP1-dependent phosphorylation of ezrin/radixin/moesin (ERM) family proteins.
source: Polar cortical relaxation has been proposed to be regulated by Aurora A kinase activity, astral microtubules, and PP1-dependent phosphorylation of ezrin/radixin/moesin (ERM) family proteins (Kunda et al., 2012; Rodrigues et al., 2015; Mangal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on polar cortical relaxation regulation.

claim: Extrinsic cell fate signaling may have direct downstream effects on the cytokinetic machinery in EMS.

evidence: This is a speculative inference from the correlation between cell-fate signaling and cytokinetic protection.

claim: Both cell fate specification and asymmetric cell division in EMS are downstream of two partially redundant signaling pathways that depend on cell-cell contact between P2 and EMS: Wnt/Frizzled and Receptor Tyrosine Kinase (RTK)/Src signaling.
source: Both cell fate specification and asymmetric cell division in EMS are downstream of two partially redundant signaling pathways that influence similar downstream targets and depend on cell-cell contact between P2 and EMS: Wnt/Frizzled and Receptor Tyrosine Kinase (RTK)/Src signaling (Goldstein, 1992, 1993, 1995a, 1995b; Rocheleau et al., 1997; Thorpe et al., 1997; Bei et al., 2002; Arata et al., 2010; Schierenberg, 1987; Sugioka and Sawa, 2010; Berkowitz and Strome, 2000).

claim: During EMS cell fate specification, the WntMOM-2 ligand from P2 activates FrizzledMOM-5 receptors on the surface of EMS.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Transmembrane-domain-containing RTKMES-1 on P2 stimulates the same RTKMES-1 on EMS in trans, promoting SrcSRC-1 activation in both cells.
source: In parallel, transmembrane-domain-containing RTKMES-1 on P2 stimulates the same RTKMES-1 on EMS in trans, promoting SrcSRC-1 activation in both cells (Bei et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2010; Sugioka and Sawa, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Both a high cell-cell contact area and proper spindle orientation are highly correlated with successful cytokinesis in EMS.
source: Indeed, we found that both a high cell-cell contact area and proper spindle orientation, two indicators of successful cell fate signaling from P2 to EMS, are highly correlated with successful cytokinesis in EMS (Figures 7 and 8), and that depletion of SrcSRC-1 specifically causes division failure in the EMS cell, but not the P2 cell.

claim: Depletion of SrcSRC-1 specifically causes division failure in the EMS cell, but not the P2 cell.
source: Indeed, we found that both a high cell-cell contact area and proper spindle orientation, two indicators of successful cell fate signaling from P2 to EMS, are highly correlated with successful cytokinesis in EMS (Figures 7 and 8), and that depletion of SrcSRC-1 specifically causes division failure in the EMS cell, but not the P2 cell.

claim: Both Wnt and Src-family kinase signaling have been implicated in both positive and negative regulations of cytokinesis in other cell contexts.
source: In support of cell-fate signaling in cytokinetic diversity, both Wnt and Src-family kinase signaling have been implicated in both positive and negative regulations of cytokinesis in other cell contexts (De Santis Puzzonia et al., 2016; Fumoto et al., 2012; Kasahara et al., 2007; Soeda et al., 2013; Kamranvar et al., 2016; Avanzi et al., 2012; Sánchez-Bailón et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2014; Ikeuchi et al., 2016; Jungas et al., 2016; Kakae et al., 2017), and in human cancer cell lines Wnt5a, its receptor FrizzledFz2, as well as a mediator of Wnt signaling, DishevelledDvl2, all localize to the midbody at the division plane (Fumoto et al., 2012; Kikuchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on Wnt and Src signaling in cytokinesis.

claim: In human cancer cell lines Wnt5a, its receptor FrizzledFz2, as well as a mediator of Wnt signaling, DishevelledDvl2, all localize to the midbody at the division plane.
source: In support of cell-fate signaling in cytokinetic diversity, both Wnt and Src-family kinase signaling have been implicated in both positive and negative regulations of cytokinesis in other cell contexts (De Santis Puzzonia et al., 2016; Fumoto et al., 2012; Kasahara et al., 2007; Soeda et al., 2013; Kamranvar et al., 2016; Avanzi et al., 2012; Sánchez-Bailón et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2014; Ikeuchi et al., 2016; Jungas et al., 2016; Kakae et al., 2017), and in human cancer cell lines Wnt5a, its receptor FrizzledFz2, as well as a mediator of Wnt signaling, DishevelledDvl2, all localize to the midbody at the division plane (Fumoto et al., 2012; Kikuchi et al., 2010).
